lead: Both readings look to the end. Second Peter says that the day of the Lord will come like a thief, and that we wait for new heavens and a new earth where righteousness is at home. In Mark, Jesus says that no one knows the day or the hour, and gives one command three times: keep awake. In these last days before the Ascension, the Church remembers that the Lord who goes up to heaven will come again, and that the time between is a time for watchful, holy living.

r.h: New heavens and a new earth
set: Second Peter is written in the name of the apostle Peter as his last testament (1:14). Many scholars think it was written by a disciple in Peter’s name some decades after his death, drawing on the Letter of Jude; others defend Petrine authorship. The Church has received it as Scripture since the fourth century, though some early writers were hesitant. In chapter 3 the writer answers scoffers who say, “Where is the promise of his coming?” (3:4). His answer: God is not slow but patient, “not wanting any to perish” (3:9).
str: v. 10: the day of the Lord comes like a thief; the heavens pass away; the earth is laid bare.
vv. 11–12: what sort of people ought you to be? Holy and godly, waiting for and hastening the day.
v. 13: according to his promise, new heavens and a new earth, where righteousness is at home.
kw: Jesus’ own image for his unexpected coming (Matthew 24:43), used also by Paul (1 Thessalonians 5:2). The point is not menace but surprise: be ready at every hour.
A bold word: Christians can “hasten” the day by holy lives, prayer and repentance. The early Church prayed Marana tha, “Our Lord, come!” (1 Corinthians 16:22).
vv: the earth and everything that is done on it will be disclosed.

Textual note: the Greek manuscripts differ here. The oldest read “will be found” (that is, laid bare before God), which the NRSV renders “disclosed”; many later manuscripts read “will be burned up”, which the POC follows. Either way, nothing will remain hidden from God.
what sort of persons ought you to be in leading lives of holiness and godliness,
The teaching about the end is never for idle speculation. It leads at once to a question about how we live now.
But, in accordance with his promise, we wait for new heavens and a new earth, where righteousness is at home.
The promise is Isaiah’s (65:17; 66:22). The end is not destruction for its own sake but renewal: a world where justice finally dwells.
ch: The Catechism cites this verse when it teaches that at the end of time the visible universe itself will be transformed, so that the world itself, restored to its original state, may be at the service of the just (CCC 1043, 1047). The Second Vatican Council adds that the expectation of a new earth must not weaken but rather stimulate our concern for cultivating this one (Gaudium et Spes 39). The Christian waits for the end by working for justice now.

set: Mark 13 is Jesus’ last long discourse before his Passion, spoken on the Mount of Olives opposite the Temple. He has foretold the Temple’s destruction and spoken of trials, false messiahs, and the coming of the Son of Man. Today’s verses end the discourse. After many signs, the final word is not a timetable but a command: keep awake.
str: v. 32: no one knows the day or hour, not even the Son, but only the Father.
v. 34: the parable of the man on a journey, the servants with their work, the doorkeeper.
vv. 35–37: keep awake: evening, midnight, cockcrow, dawn; what I say to you I say to all.
kw: Literally “do not sleep”, to stay wakeful through the night.
Used three times in vv. 34–37. In Gethsemane Jesus will ask Peter, James and John to “keep awake” with the same verb, and will find them sleeping (14:34–37).
vv: But about that day or hour no one knows, neither the angels in heaven, nor the Son, but only the Father.
A verse the Church has always taken seriously (see the question below). It forbids every attempt to calculate the date of the end.
Watching is not idleness. The servants keep watch by doing the work each has been given.
in the evening, or at midnight, or at cockcrow, or at dawn,

The four watches of the night in the Roman reckoning. Mark’s Passion story moves through the same hours: the supper in the evening (14:17), Gethsemane in the night, Peter’s denial at cockcrow (14:72), and the handing over to Pilate at dawn (15:1).
And what I say to you I say to all: Keep awake.”
The command is not only for the four disciples on the mountain but for the whole Church in every age.
ch: The Catechism explains that Christ’s human knowledge, united to the divine wisdom of the Word, enjoyed the fullness of understanding of the eternal plans he had come to reveal; what he said he did not know in this matter, he elsewhere declared he was not sent to reveal (CCC 474). The Church therefore never sets dates for the end, but lives each day in watchful hope (CCC 673).

qa: How can the Son not know the day or the hour?

The Church teaches that Jesus has a true human mind as well as his divine nature. Some Fathers explain the verse by his human knowledge; others say he did not know it as something he had come to reveal. The Catechism teaches that in his human knowledge, joined to the divine wisdom, Christ knew the eternal plans fully, and that what he said he did not know, he was not sent to reveal (CCC 474). The verse teaches us humility: the date belongs to the Father.
study: Second Peter asks, “what sort of persons ought you to be?” What would I change in my life if I took the Lord’s coming seriously today?
In the parable each servant keeps watch by doing his own work. What work has the Lord given me to do while I wait for him?
